notes:
I've put together notes for vv. 1–21 below. Coverage is uneven. Enduring Word (Guzik), the bible.org exegetical commentary and Wesley's Notes give the most verse-by-verse detail. Most of the denominational and other views I found are about vv. 10, 11–15 and 16. **What I couldn't find:** any Lutheran or Orthodox commentary (the oca.org page I found only has the Bible text), any Catholic reading other than on v. 16, and notes on vv. 19–21 beyond a short summary. Those are left out.

**Context (vv. 1–21)**
- The bible.org commentary says vv. 1–21 carry on Jesus' words to the Pharisees from 9:41. Chapter 9 acts out the parable: the Pharisees threw the healed blind man out, while Jesus found him and led him to safety. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- It names Ezekiel 34 as the most important Old Testament background, along with Numbers 27:15–18. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10

**v. 1**
- Guzik: rulers were often called "shepherds" in the ancient world. One mark of a thief is how he gets in among the sheep. He says the religious leaders got their place through connections, schooling, ambition and corruption. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik): anyone who enters the pastor's office for any motive other than Christ and his people, such as ambition, greed or love of ease, is a thief and a robber. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- MacArthur: the verse describes the Pharisees as false shepherds who have no right to the sheep they fleece. https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-52/i-am-the-door
- Bible.org: the fold is probably a courtyard in front of a house, with a stone wall around it. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10

**v. 2**
- Guzik: a true shepherd comes in the proper way, through love, calling, care and sacrificial service. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/

**v. 3**
- **Who is the gatekeeper? Interpreters disagree.**
  - Wesley says it isn't beneath God the Father to be called the doorkeeper. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-10.html
  - Clarke (via Guzik) sees the Holy Spirit opening the way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
  - Bible.org finds no attempt to identify him convincing. It treats him as a detail of the story with no symbolic meaning. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- Guzik: in towns, several flocks often shared one fold, guarded by a single doorkeeper. Calling sheep by name shows a personal bond. The shepherd leads rather than drives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Bible.org: Palestinian shepherds often gave favourite sheep pet names. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10

**v. 4**
- Wesley: the shepherd goes ahead by example as well as teaching. The sheep know his voice because they have an inner witness that his words are God's wisdom and power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm
- Guzik retells a story of a shepherd near Jerusalem who called back his stolen flock with his voice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Bible.org: some think several flocks shared the fold and were separated by the shepherd's call. It adds that John never divides the sheep (compare v. 16). https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10

**v. 5**
- Piper (Baptist) identifies the "stranger" with the Pharisees, who did not have the Gatekeeper's blessing. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/my-abandoned-life-for-your-abundant-life--2

**v. 6**
- Wesley: "they" means the Pharisees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm
- Bible.org: John's word for "illustration" is close to the other Gospels' "parable." The listeners' failure to understand is one of John's literary techniques, and they could not understand because they were not his sheep (v. 26). https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- Desiring God uses this verse as proof that the whole passage, including v. 10, is figurative. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-gods-of-the-prosperity-gospel

**v. 7**
- Guzik: in field pens the shepherd lay across the single opening, so he was literally the door. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Wesley: Christ is both the door and the shepherd. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm
- Bible.org counts this as the third of Jesus' seven "I am" sayings. https://bible.org/series/24-ways-?page=1461

**v. 8**
- Bible.org: this cannot mean the Old Testament prophets, given 5:46 and 8:56. The present tense ("are") points to the religious leaders of Jesus' own day. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- Guzik (citing Morris, Tasker and Trapp) agrees. He notes that the early heretic Manes used the verse against Moses and the prophets, and that Augustine replied they came *with* Christ, not before him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/

**v. 9**
- Wesley: "enters" means through faith, and the person is safe from the wolf. "Pasture" is food for the soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-10.html
- Guzik (citing Dods): "go in and out" is an Old Testament phrase for the freedom of everyday life. Dods also suggests the words first comforted the excommunicated blind man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Bible.org links "pasture" to Ezekiel 34 and reads the verse as Jesus being the way into the Kingdom. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10

**v. 10**
- Guzik (citing Clarke): a thief works by stealth, a robber by violence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Guzik (citing Boice): abundant life is not mainly a long or easy life but contentment in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- **Is there more and less of this life?**
  - Spurgeon taught that "life is a matter of degrees": believers grow in grace and so have life "more abundantly." https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/blog-entries/sermon-of-the-week-no-1150-life-more-abundant/
  - Bible.org disagrees with reading the verse as levels within eternal life. It sees only the overflowing quality of that life. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- **Prosperity teaching (debated):**
  - Desiring God says prosperity teachers cite this verse but read figurative language literally. In John, "life" almost always means eternal life. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-gods-of-the-prosperity-gospel
  - Ligonier: the verse is not about luxury or "your best life now." The best is yet to come. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/what-does-john-10-mean
  - GotQuestions: Jesus' own definition of eternal life (John 17:3) says nothing about health or wealth. https://www.gotquestions.org/abundant-life.html
  - Another article on ccel.org is partly sympathetic. Beneath the movement's distortions, it sees a real witness that God cares about the poor's material conditions. https://ccel.org/node/13394

**v. 11**
- Gill: Christ gives his life freely, in the sheep's place, as a ransom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-11.htm
- Calvin: Christ gave his life to pay for sin, and to set an example for his ministers. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol34/htm/xvi.iii.htm
- NET note: "good" can mean "model." Jesus has his own substitutionary death in view. A real shepherd's death would doom the flock, but here it brings them life. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Joh+10%3A11-16%2C26%2C27
- Carson (TGC): this is a messianic claim. To those with ears to hear, it says Yahweh himself is the Good Shepherd. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/part-6-jesus-the-shepherd-of-god-john-10-1-21/
- Barclay: Greek *kalos* adds loveliness to goodness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-10.html
- **Whom did Christ die for? (Protestant disagreement on vv. 11, 15)**
  - Reformed: Ligonier says he laid down his life only for his sheep, which guaranteed their salvation. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/particular-atonement
  - Joel Beeke (monergism.com) says "for" means a definite exchange. https://www.monergism.com/definite-atonement
  - Kevin DeYoung (TGC) puts it as "not for the goats, but for the sheep." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/kevin-deyoung/theological-primer-limited-atonement/
  - Methodist/Arminian: Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik at v. 16) says Christ tasted death "for every man." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
  - The Restoration Movement commentator Coffman says Jesus willingly died "for men." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-11.html

**vv. 12–13**
- Wesley: the hired hand runs because he loves the wages, not the sheep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm
- Guzik (citing Alford): the wolf is the same enemy as the thief, the great foe of Christ's sheep. Spurgeon called pastors who won't oppose false teaching hirelings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- NET note: "he runs away" in v. 13 is missing from several important manuscripts and was probably added later. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Joh+10%3A11-16%2C26%2C27

**vv. 14–15**
- Wesley: Christ knows his sheep with tender care, and they know him with holy confidence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: knowing implies affection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_010.cfm
- Bible.org: Jesus compares his bond with the sheep to his bond with the Father. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- Piper: Jesus is bound to his sheep as he is bound to his Father. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/my-abandoned-life-for-your-abundant-life--2
- On "lay down my life for the sheep" (v. 15), see the atonement disagreement under v. 11.

**v. 16**
- The "other sheep" are Gentiles: Wesley (who adds "which he foreknew") https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm; NET https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Joh+10%3A11-16%2C26%2C27; Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Wesley notes the text says one *flock*, not one *fold*, and calls "fold" a misprint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/10.htm
- Spurgeon made the same correction in a sermon. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/other-sheep-and-one-flock
- Dods (via Guzik): nothing here requires one organisation; there may be several folds but one flock. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Bible.org: the unity is created by Jesus, not something that already exists. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- **Catholic view:** the "one flock, one shepherd" subsists in the Catholic Church, governed by Peter's successor (*Dominus Iesus* 17). https://www.catholic.com/qa/when-jesus-mentioned-the-one-flock-one-shepherd-was-he-referring-to-the-catholic-church-alone

**v. 17**
- Bible.org: the Father loves the Son for his complete obedience, even to death. In John, that death is completed by resurrection and return to the Father. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10

**v. 18**
- Bible.org: his death was voluntary (compare 19:11). The authority came from the Father. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- Oswald Chambers (via Precept Austin): this was no act of impulse; it was chosen freely, with full knowledge, and with no chance of escape. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-10-commentary

**vv. 19–21**
- Bible.org: in v. 6 the response was confusion; now it is division. The charge of demon-possession repeats chapter 8, and v. 21 looks back to the blind man. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-exegetical-commentary-john-10
- Guzik: Jesus' words were supreme sanity, not madness, and his deeds were utterly unselfish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- Piper: anyone who claims authority to take his life up again after death is either insane or God. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/my-abandoned-life-for-your-abundant-life--2
